hints: Look closely at the direction of water potential change in option A. Does adding more solute (sucrose) make water potential higher or lower (more negative)?
Remember how sucrose gets into the phloem at a leaf against its concentration gradient. What energy-requiring transport using hydrogen ions and a co-transporter protein is involved?
walkthrough:
**Recall the big picture of mass flow**

Think source to sink. At the source, sucrose is loaded in. Water follows by osmosis. This builds high hydrostatic pressure that pushes sap toward the sink.

Key rule:
$$\text{more solute} \rightarrow \text{lower (more negative) water potential } (\Psi) \rightarrow \text{water enters}$$

**Focus on loading at the source**

Sucrose is made in the photosynthesising leaf and must be moved into the phloem against a concentration gradient. This cannot be diffusion.

Hydrogen ions are first pumped out of the companion cell using ATP. Then H+ flow back in together with sucrose through a co-transporter protein. This is active loading by co-transport.

**Test each statement**

Option A gets water potential backwards. Option B puts starch formation in the wrong place. Option C names the wrong transport mechanism. Only option D correctly describes the H+ and sucrose co-transporter into the companion cell.

options.A: Adding sucrose lowers (makes more negative) water potential, it does not increase it. Water then enters by osmosis and raises hydrostatic pressure.
options.B: Sucrose is unloaded at the sink, but polymerisation into starch happens later inside the storage cells, not inside the sieve tube element itself.
options.C: Loading at the source is against a concentration gradient so needs active transport by co-transport, not facilitated diffusion which is passive.
options.D: Correct. At the source, sucrose is actively loaded into companion cells (then moves to sieve tubes) by a sucrose-H+ co-transporter protein using a hydrogen ion gradient.
